sermons.life_context: Newly engaged as pastor at Bolton, Connecticut, having agreed on 11 November 1723 to settle there, two months after receiving his M.A. at New Haven; his New York City pulpit had ended that April. The WJE editor suggests the sermon's references to 'this town' may reflect quarrels during Bolton's several-year search for a minister. He left Bolton in May 1724 to become a Yale tutor.

Senior pastor at Northampton, Massachusetts, since his grandfather Solomon Stoddard died in February 1729, after which he fell ill that spring and suffered a physical collapse in June. He had married Sarah Pierpont in July 1727, and their first children were born from 1728. The WJE editor links the sermon to Northampton's factional rivalry over land and town offices such as selectman.

Senior pastor at Northampton since his grandfather Solomon Stoddard's death in February 1729, he preached this in Boston to a meeting of clergy, having first given it at Northampton in fall 1730. Printed soon afterwards with a preface by Thomas Prince and William Cooper, it became his first published work.

Senior pastor at Northampton since his grandfather Solomon Stoddard's death in February 1729, and married to Sarah Pierpont since July 1727, with their first children born from 1728. The WJE editor connects the sermon to widening economic divisions in the town. It is the first sermon Edwards dated.

Senior pastor at Northampton since February 1729, he preached this to his own congregation before the Connecticut Valley revivals began there in December 1734. According to the WJE editor, its publication in Boston the following year enhanced his reputation.

Pastor at Northampton since 1727 and senior pastor since 1729, he gave this as a Northampton lecture about a month before the Connecticut Valley revivals began among his congregation in December 1734. He later roughly doubled it for publication in 1738, when it opened his Discourses on Various Important Subjects.

Pastor at Northampton during the revival that began among his congregation in December 1734 and that he later described in A Faithful Narrative (London, 1737). The WJE editor places the sermon about ten weeks after his November 1734 lecture on justification and within five weeks of the revival's start.

Pastor at Northampton in 1736, the closing year of the revival period a WJE editor dates 1734–36; his account of that revival, A Faithful Narrative, was published in London the following year. In his 1738 preface Edwards said he had preached this sermon in another town, whose people asked for a copy.

Pastor at Northampton in the year A Faithful Narrative, his account of the town's revival, was published in London. The WJE editor ties the sermon to a divisive debate over the new meetinghouse and the town's response to the collapse of the meetinghouse galleries, and sees in it a possible early sign of the rift that later divided him from his church, which dismissed him in 1750.

Through these months he was pastor at Northampton, at a point the WJE editor places about midway through his ministry there and between the revivals of 1734–36 and 1740–43. In 1738 a corrected Boston edition of A Faithful Narrative appeared, and his Discourses on Various Important Subjects was published.

Pastor at Northampton in 1740, the first year of the awakening of 1740–42; two months later, in October 1740, he hosted George Whitefield there for three days. The sermon followed a special meeting for young people in July, and in a 1743 letter Edwards reported that by mid-December 1740 a considerable work had appeared among the very young.

Pastor at Northampton, he was preaching widely during the regional awakening of 1740–42, nine months after hosting George Whitefield in October 1740. He had given an earlier version to his own congregation in June; two months later he would defend the revivals at Yale's commencement.

Still pastor at Northampton, he addressed the commencement of the college where he had studied and tutored, two months after preaching at Enfield during the 1740–42 awakening. The WJE editor notes that the itinerant James Davenport had just left New Haven after publicly denouncing its pastor Joseph Noyes, and that many were asking whether the revival could be controlled or defended.

Pastor at Northampton, he had cared for the missionary David Brainerd, who died of tuberculosis in the Edwards home on 9 October 1747; this was the funeral sermon three days later. Edwards went on to edit Brainerd's Life (1749). His daughter Jerusha, who had helped nurse Brainerd, died of a fever four months afterwards.

Nine days earlier, on 22 June 1750, Northampton had dismissed him as pastor after church councils over his stricter qualifications for communion, ending a conflict with his church that began in 1749. He had served there since 1726 and lost his daughter Jerusha in 1748. Afterwards he did supply preaching at Northampton and elsewhere until Stockbridge called him in February 1751.
